subject: chemistry
title: Transition elements and their properties
key_idea: A transition element is a d-block element that forms at least one stable ion with an incomplete d sub-shell. That incomplete d sub-shell gives four typical properties: complex formation, coloured ions, variable oxidation states and catalytic activity.

blocks.text: This section covers how to write the configurations of Period 4 d-block atoms and ions, from scandium to zinc.

items: The 4s sub-shell fills before the 3d sub-shell, because 4s is lower in energy in the atom.
Argon is 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶. Write [Ar] for this core, then add 3d and 4s.
Iron: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁶4s², or [Ar] 3d⁶4s².
Chromium and copper are exceptions. Cr is [Ar] 3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is [Ar] 3d¹⁰4s¹. A half-filled or full 3d sub-shell is more stable.
When a d-block atom forms a positive ion, the **4s electrons are lost first**, then 3d electrons.
Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶. Fe³⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁵.
Cu²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁹. Cu⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰.
Zn²⁺ is [Ar] 3d¹⁰. Sc³⁺ is [Ar], with no d electrons.

items.text: Cobalt, atomic number 27, has 27 electrons. Co²⁺ has 25.
Fill up to argon (18), then 4s², then 3d⁷ for the atom: [Ar] 3d⁷4s².
Take away two electrons from 4s: Co²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁷.

items: Fill 4s before 3d, but remove 4s electrons first when forming ions.
Cr is 3d⁵4s¹ and Cu is 3d¹⁰4s¹.
Count the electrons in the ion, not the atom.

blocks.text: The definition depends on the ion, not on the atom. This section covers the definition and why scandium and zinc are left out.

items.meaning: A d-block element that forms one or more stable ions with an incomplete d sub-shell.
An element whose highest-energy electron is in a d sub-shell.

items: Scandium only forms Sc³⁺, which has an empty d sub-shell.
Zinc only forms Zn²⁺, which has a full d sub-shell.
Neither has an ion with an **incomplete d sub-shell**, so neither is a transition element.
The transition elements are titanium to copper.

diagram.alt: Sort each ion into transition element or not a transition element, using its d electrons.
diagram.prompt: Each element forms the ion shown. Does that element count as a transition element?

items: Transition elements form an ion with an incomplete d sub-shell.
Scandium and zinc are d-block elements but not transition elements.
Copper counts because Cu²⁺ is 3d⁹, even though Cu⁺ is 3d¹⁰.

blocks.text: The incomplete d sub-shell gives four characteristic properties. Each has its own note later in this chapter.

rows: Cu²⁺(aq) is blue, Fe³⁺(aq) is yellow-brown
Iron forms Fe²⁺ and Fe³⁺; vanadium forms +2 to +5
Iron in the Haber process, V₂O₅ in the Contact process

items.meaning: A molecule or ion that donates a lone pair of electrons to a central metal atom or ion, forming a coordinate (dative covalent) bond.
A central metal atom or ion surrounded by one or more ligands.
The number of coordinate bonds to the central metal atom or ion.

items: **Variable oxidation states:** the 3d and 4s sub-shells are very close in energy. Electrons can be lost from both, so several stable ions form.
**Complexes and catalysis:** the d sub-shell has vacant d orbitals at accessible energy. They can accept lone pairs from ligands and bind reactants.
**Colour:** electrons can move between d orbitals that have been split in energy by the ligands.
Four properties: complexes, colour, variable oxidation states, catalysis.
Close 3d and 4s energies explain the variable oxidation states.
Vacant, accessible d orbitals explain complex formation and catalysis.

checks.q: Write the electron configuration of Fe³⁺ using sub-shell notation.
checks.a: 1s²2s²2p⁶3s²3p⁶3d⁵ (or [Ar] 3d⁵). The two 4s electrons and one 3d electron are lost from [Ar] 3d⁶4s².

checks.q: Explain why zinc is a d-block element but not a transition element.
checks.a: Zinc only forms the Zn²⁺ ion. Zn²⁺ has a full 3d sub-shell (3d¹⁰), so it has no ion with an incomplete d sub-shell.

checks.q: Explain why transition elements show variable oxidation states.
checks.a: The 3d and 4s sub-shells are very close in energy, so electrons from both can be lost. This allows ions with different charges, each reasonably stable.

items: Illustrate the properties with at least two transition elements, such as iron and copper.
Practical examples of catalytic behaviour: Cu²⁺ in the reaction of zinc with acids, and MnO₂ in the decomposition of H₂O₂.
Catalysts of transition elements and their compounds matter in the industrial manufacture of chemicals.

blocks.text: Two of the five 3d orbitals have shapes you must be able to sketch.

items: **3dxy:** four lobes, lying between the x and y axes in the xy plane.
**3dz²:** two lobes along the z axis, with a ring (doughnut) of electron density around the nucleus in the xy plane.
In an isolated atom the five 3d orbitals have the same energy. They are **degenerate**.
Vacant 3d orbitals that are close in energy to 4s are energetically accessible, so they can form dative bonds with ligands.
